content: Forceps are handheld, hinged instruments designed for grasping and holding objects. They are particularly useful when fingers are too large to handle small objects or when multiple objects need to be held simultaneously while performing a task. The term forceps is predominantly used in the medical field, whereas outside of medicine, similar tools are often referred to as tweezers, tongs, pliers, clips, or clamps. It is important to note that the word forceps is both singular and plural, and it is never referred to as forcep or a pair of forceps, unlike scissors. The term originates from the Latin word forca, meaning a snare or trap. Forceps made for non-surgical purposes may use lower-quality steel. Disposable forceps, intended for single use, are often made of plastic. There are two primary categories of forceps: non-locking forceps (commonly referred to as thumb forceps or pick-ups) and locking forceps. Both types are available in numerous specialized forms tailored for specific applications. Non-locking forceps are further divided into two basic designs. The first type is hinged at one end, away from the grasping end, and is colloquially referred to as tweezers, though medical professionals typically avoid this term. The second type is hinged in the middle, resembling scissors, but with flat, grasping surfaces instead of blades. Locking forceps, on the other hand, are almost always hinged in the middle, though some designs place the hinge closer to the grasping end. These forceps feature mechanisms that lock the grasping surfaces in a closed position, enabling them to clamp, grasp, or hold objects independently. Thumb Forceps Thumb forceps are designed to be held between the thumb and two or three fingers of one hand, with the top end resting on the anatomical snuffbox at the base of the thumb and index finger. These forceps are commonly used to hold tissue in place during suturing, to gently move tissues during exploratory surgery, or to handle dressings and drapes without direct hand contact. Thumb forceps may have smooth tips, cross-hatched tips, or serrated tips, often referred to as mouse's teeth. Common configurations of teeth include 1x2 (one tooth on one side interlocking with two teeth on the other), 7x7, and 9x9. Conversely, smooth or cross-hatched forceps are used for tasks such as moving dressings or removing sutures. Adson Tissue Forceps Adson tissue forceps are a specific type of thumb forceps characterized by their 1x2 mouse's teeth at the lower tip, which provide a secure grip on tissue. Locking Forceps Locking forceps, also known as clamps, are used to grasp and hold objects or tissues securely. When employed to compress an artery and control bleeding, they are referred to as hemostats. Another common type of locking forceps is the needle holder, which is used to guide a suturing needle through tissue. Most locking forceps feature finger loops to facilitate handling. These loops are typically held with the thumb and middle or ring fingers, while the index finger provides guidance. The locking mechanism usually consists of interlocking teeth located near the finger loops. As the forceps are closed, the teeth engage, preventing the grasping surfaces from separating. A simple shift of the fingers disengages the teeth, allowing the forceps to open. Locking forceps are widely used in surgical procedures. Kelly Forceps Kelly forceps are a type of locking forceps that feature a toothed locking mechanism near the finger loops. They are shown in both closed and open positions, demonstrating their functionality. Forceps in Childbirth Forceps can also be utilized during childbirth to assist in the delivery of a baby. This method serves as an alternative to the ventouse (vacuum extraction) technique.
